subject: Connection blueprint: low-touch access to private inference
messages:
From: Julia Park <julia.park@greenline.com>
To: soojin_lee@redwood.ai
Date: 2028-04-11T09:04:00Z
Subject: Access options for Redwood Private deployment

Hi Soojin,

Thanks for the quick intro last week. We're making progress on our Private deployment evaluation and want to lock down the network approach before we spin up VMs. High-level constraints:

- HIPAA-sensitive traffic (PHI) — must stay within private connectivity (no public endpoints).
- Expected baseline: 200 req/s with occasional bursts to 500 req/s during daytime. Typical request size: 1–2k tokens.
- Target p95 latency <= 120ms for inference (model hosted in us-west-2).
- We prefer a low-ops path the first quarter, but want a growth plan for sustained throughput.

Attached is our current topology diagram and the internal security checklist. Can you outline tradeoffs between VPC peering, PrivateLink (endpoint services), and site-to-site VPN for this use case? In particular: how each option affects latency, operational complexity, cross-account security boundaries, and egress/cost considerations.

Would also like to know if streaming (server-sent events) and persistent KV cache usage (for long context windows) are impacted by the connectivity choice.

Thanks — can we sync this week?

Julia Park
Director of Cloud Platforms | Greenline Health
Julia.Park@greenline.com
+1 415 555 0199

Attachment: greenline_current_topology.pdf
From: Soojin Lee <soojin_lee@redwood.ai>
To: Julia Park <julia.park@greenline.com>
Cc: karthik_iyer@redwood.ai, marissa_cole@redwood.ai
Date: 2028-04-11T13:22:00Z
Subject: Re: Access options for Redwood Private deployment

Hi Julia — thanks for the topology and clear constraints. I pulled in Karthik (networking lead) and Marissa (solutions) to give a short, practical comparison and a recommended path depending on your priorities. TL;DR: PrivateLink-first for low-touch, peering or Transit Gateway for sustained low-latency data plane, and VPN only for quick proofs or very low-throughput on-prem sites.

Quick comparison (practical bullets):

- VPC Peering
  - Pros: Native L3 routing; no proxy; minimal per-packet overhead so latency tends to be lowest in-region.
  - Cons: Cross-account peering is not transitive; route table changes required; peering across VPCs in different AWS accounts or regions can be cumbersome. Harder to apply strict service-level IAM controls — security boundaries are broader.
  - Ops: Moderate (route management, peering acceptance). Good when both sides are large AWS accounts with steady traffic.

- PrivateLink (AWS Endpoint Service)
  - Pros: Clean service boundary (L4): your VPC connects to a private endpoint, no route-table surgery required. Works across accounts and keeps the service owner control-plane in Redwood. Endpoint DNS + NLB gives per-AZ failover. Easier to audit and to enforce a least-privilege perimeter.
  - Cons: Slightly higher per-request latency versus flat peering (few ms typical), and per-endpoint data processing / hourly endpoint costs. Throughput is robust for typical inference workloads but needs sizing (NLB and ENI limits) for sustained high concurrency.
  - Ops: Low for customers (we manage the endpoint service). Recommended for customers who want minimal network ops and tighter security boundaries.

- Site-to-site VPN (IPSec)
  - Pros: Quick to provision for proof-of-concept; works for on-prem and multicloud.
  - Cons: Lower and variable throughput; higher p95 due to encapsulation, MTU issues, and potential NAT/TCP interactions. For high-throughput inference it's brittle without BGP and redundant tunnels.
  - Ops: High if you require HA and throughput. Not recommended as the long-term data plane for heavy inference workloads.

Edge recommendations for Greenline's constraints: 

1) For the low-ops first phase: PrivateLink endpoint service for model endpoints + Private DNS. Keeps PHI on private RFC1918 addresses, avoids public IPs, and minimizes any route table or NACL work on your side.

2) For sustained low-latency heavy traffic (>300–400 req/s sustained): consider Transit Gateway or direct VPC peering between your inference VPC and Redwood's data VPC in us-west-2 (we can publish an acceptance flow). Transit Gateway simplifies many-peer topologies and supports prefix limits better than multiple peering links.

3) Hybrid: Start with PrivateLink for control & small-scale testing, then add a peered data plane (or TGW) for bulk traffic once baseline throughput is validated. Use PrivateLink for administrative/control channels and peering/TGW for high-throughput inference streams.

Streaming and KV cache considerations:
- Server-side streaming (chunked SSE/websockets) works fine over PrivateLink and peering. PrivateLink will add minimal extra hops — we measure microseconds to single-digit ms overhead internally.
- Large KV cache traffic (frequent cache fills) benefits from flatter routing (peering/TGW) due to lower overhead on per-packet processing; if you expect heavy cache traffic, plan peering/TGW for the data plane.

Next steps for us:
- Can you share typical p50/p95 payload sizes and a short 24–48h traffic sample?
- If you like, we can run a short perf test (we host a canary model) to measure p95 over PrivateLink vs peering from your VPC.

I've attached a short checklist for connection readiness. Karthik — can you add a couple quick implementation notes and any hard limits we should flag?

Thanks,

— Soojin Lee
Sr. Solutions Architect | Redwood Inference
soojin_lee@redwood.ai

Attachment: redwood_connection_checklist.md
From: Karthik Iyer <karthik_iyer@redwood.ai>

Cc: marissa_cole@redwood.ai, ben_carter@redwood.ai
Date: 2028-04-12T10:03:00Z
Subject: Re: Access options for Redwood Private deployment — implementation notes

Adding implementation details and hard limits we typically hit so Greenline can plan: 

- PrivateLink sizing
  - NLB + Endpoint ENIs: endpoints create one or more ENIs per AZ; account ENI limits can be a blocker. We'll ask for your account ENI quota before we provision.
  - Throughput: PrivateLink performs well for concurrent HTTP streams; for extremely high sustained connections (>1 Gbps per endpoint) you should plan multiple endpoints across AZs and possibly split traffic by model.

- VPC Peering / TGW
  - Peering does not support transitive routing — if you have multiple VPCs, TGW is usually simpler.
  - Route table scale: if you have many subnets/VPCs, route table entries and propagation have operational costs.

- VPN specifics (on-prem)
  - If Greenline needs on-prem access, prefer BGP-enabled HA tunnels with MTU 1400 and monitor for TCP retransmits when large response payloads are returned.

- Ports and health checks
  - Our inference service uses 443/HTTPS for API traffic; health checks from NLB are simple TCP/HTTP health probes. If you plan to front with a proxy/NGINX, ensure idle timeouts >= 90s for long streaming responses.

- Security / auditability
  - PrivateLink makes it easy to log endpoint acceptance flows and centralize AWS CloudTrail entries. Peering bundles traffic into VPC-level logs which can be noisier.

- Cost note
  - PrivateLink has per-GB data processing + endpoint-hour charges; peering has data transfer charges between AZs/accounts depending on region. We can run a quick cost model once you share expected GB/month.

I'm attaching a quick cost estimator I used for a similar customer. Ben — if you have example numbers from Cobalt (without PII) please paste them.

— Karthik

Thanks Soojin & Karthik — this is helpful. A couple follow-ups from our network/security team: 

- Can you confirm PrivateLink supports streaming gRPC/HTTP2 patterns (we use chunked responses for real-time transcription)?
- If we go PrivateLink-first, how do we do a canary for one model variant and then fail over to peered data plane later? Any config we need to pre-provision?
- Rough estimate: we expect ~5 TB/month egress initially, growing to ~20 TB over 12 months. Please flag any cost cliffs.

We can do a 30-min call Thursday to walk through the checklist and what you need from us. Proposed attendees from our side: myself (network), Julia (cloud platform), R&D lead (TBD).

Thanks,
Michael

Date: 2028-04-13T15:12:00Z
Subject: Re: Access options for Redwood Private deployment — scheduling

Thanks — short answers and action items before the call: 

- PrivateLink & streaming: supported. We proxy HTTP/2 and chunked SSE through our NLB; we recommend an idle timeout >= 90s and keepalive tuning on client side.
- Canary pattern: we recommend configuring Private DNS with weighted CNAMEs for a canary model, or split at the application layer: direct a % of requests to a peered endpoint once peering/TGW is active. We'll provide a runbook for DNS-weighted cutovers.
- Cost cliffs: initial 5 TB/month is comfortably within typical PrivateLink cost bands; 20 TB/month starts to favor peering/TGW from a unit-cost perspective. We'll run numbers for both and surface threshold.

Call: Thursday 2028-04-14 16:00 PT / 23:00 UTC — proposed 30 minutes. Confirm attendees and we'll send an invite with agenda (checklist + perf test plan). Pre-call ask: please attach a 48h traffic sample (p50/p95 sizes) and your AWS account ENI quota so Karhtik can pre-check.

Best,
— Soojin
Sr. Solutions Architect | Redwood Inference
